facts.claim: A bezel setting holds the stone with a thin metal rim that wraps the girdle; a full bezel encircles the whole edge for maximum protection.

GIA says bezel settings resist chips and everyday wear well, their smooth edges are less likely to catch on clothing or gloves, and it names them a practical choice for people who work with their hands or have an active lifestyle.
Bezels cover more of the stone's edge than prongs and let slightly less light into the stone.
A partial (half) bezel leaves sections of the stone exposed while still adding security; GIA describes it as balancing visibility and protection.
GIA recommends bezels, partial bezels or V-shaped prongs to protect vulnerable points and corners from chipping.
A flush setting sets the stone into the band so its top sits level with the metal surface; it is low profile, highly durable and unlikely to catch on clothing or gloves.
Flush-set rings usually need wider, thicker shanks to accommodate the stone's size and depth, and let in less light than bezel or prong settings.
GIA's gemstone durability guidance says flush setting is best used for durable stones (such as diamonds) because of the stress created during the setting process.
Prong settings let the most light into the stone, but prongs should be checked occasionally and their raised edges can catch on fabrics.

Six prongs hold a diamond more securely than four: if one of four prongs shears off the stone can fall out, whereas with six the stone is likely to stay in place; six prongs also protect the girdle better.
GIA suggests having engagement ring prongs checked every six months, or at least yearly (for example on the wedding anniversary).
Bent or broken prongs can expose vulnerable areas to chipping, and a loose diamond can even cut through metal prongs and fall out.
Worn prongs may need re-tipping (rebuilding worn tips by adding metal), and stones may need tightening over time.

A compass-set (east-west) head places four prongs at the 12, 3, 6 and 9 o'clock positions rather than at the corners. Definition only, from a jeweller's technical page; no gemmological body source found for any durability benefit.
A tension setting suspends the stone between the open ends of the band using engineered pressure; it is mostly used with hard stones such as diamond and sapphire.
Tension settings leave the stone more exposed than bezel or channel settings, careful wear is recommended, and a hard blow can shift or loosen the stone.
Tension-set rings can be very difficult, and sometimes impossible, to resize.
facts.conflicts: Jeweller pages (danhov.com, jewelry-auctioned.com) say true tension rings generally cannot be resized and are made to exact size. Use GIA wording: 'very difficult, sometimes impossible'.

facts.claim: Many rings sold as 'tension style' actually hold the stone with hidden prongs or a partial bezel; a true tension setting relies on the metal's pressure alone. Definition only, from a jeweller's technical page; describe in our own words.
A channel setting holds a row of stones between two parallel metal walls; the stones are protected by the metal, durable and suited to everyday wear, and less likely to catch than prong-set accents.
Channel-set rings can be difficult to resize, especially when stones run far around the band.
GIA notes channel settings protect sidestones by keeping them flush.

A bar setting holds stones between vertical metal bars, letting light in from the sides; bar-set stones are more exposed than channel-set ones and may be slightly more vulnerable to impact or chipping, though the bars still give good security.
Bar-set rings, like channel-set rings, can be harder to resize when stones extend far around the band.
A basket setting is a prong setting with horizontal supports linking the prongs beneath the stone, which stabilises the prongs and helps stop them bending or spreading.

Cathedral styles use metal arches that raise the centre stone higher above the band; GIA notes the elevated structure may be more likely to catch on clothing or objects, though the arches add stability.
Halo and pavé designs contain many small stones and may need more maintenance to keep stones secure and clean; pavé bands can be harder to resize.
GIA says some settings need less upkeep and suit active lifestyles; more open or delicate designs such as prong and pavé benefit from periodic inspection.
GIA advises taking the ring off before gardening or other risky activities, noting that exercise, catching on clothing and accidental knocks all take their toll.
Mohs hardness measures scratch resistance and is not linear: diamond is 10 and ruby/sapphire (corundum) 9, yet diamond is many times harder; only a diamond can scratch a diamond.
Durability depends on hardness, toughness and stability; diamond is the hardest gem but not the toughest and can be cleaved or fractured by a hard blow, breaking more easily along cleavage planes.
Diamonds with very thin girdles or exposed points (pear, marquise) are more prone to chipping; V-shaped prongs help protect pointed corners on heart, princess, pear and marquise cuts.
Moissanite is 9.25 on the Mohs scale; sapphire and ruby are 9.

Morganite is 7.5 to 8 on the Mohs scale and needs more care than diamond or sapphire; emerald is 7.5 to 8 but is not a tough gem, often has surface-reaching fractures and is often treated with oil or resin.
GIA's coloured gemstone guide says spinel, morganite, zircon, tsavorite and tourmaline can be worn daily with care, adding 'no rock climbing'.
Sudden extreme temperature changes (thermal shock) can create or spread fractures and cleavages, even in diamond.
GIA describes platinum as very wear resistant and durable; it develops a patina over time that can be polished away.

White gold is usually rhodium plated; the plating wears away gradually, the ring can start to look warmer in colour, and it needs replating from time to time. Some platinum rings are also rhodium plated and then need replating too.
Gold's durability depends on karat and alloy: higher karat gold is purer, softer and more prone to scratches and dents.

Chlorine can erode some metal alloys used in diamond settings, possibly damaging or loosening prongs, so GIA advises removing diamond jewellery before a chlorinated pool or hot tub. GIA also states chlorine can damage gold mountings.
GIA advises packing jewellery in carry-on luggage rather than checked bags, and telling your insurer your travel dates when travelling with jewellery.
GIA suggests storing each piece separately in a padded box or soft pouch, and keeping diamonds away from softer gems they could scratch.
GIA advises checking that a jewellery insurance policy covers damage and loss as well as theft, and reading it carefully.
The Jewellers Association of Australia says most valuations are for insurance and recommends jewellery be revalued approximately every 2 years.
Some popular destinations and activities can be hard on jewellery; GIA suggests leaving fragile pieces or softer gems at home or packing them carefully.

insider_details.detail: Book a prong and setting check four to six weeks before flying to a destination wedding, so any re-tipping or tightening is done with time to spare; GIA's own guide is every six months.
If the ring is mostly prong-set, ask for six claws or a basket gallery: a single sheared claw on a four-claw head is the classic lost-stone scenario.
For a resort week, take the ring off before the hotel pool or spa and leave it in a padded pouch in the room safe; chlorine is hard on the alloys that hold claws.
Ring travels in the carry-on, never checked luggage, and the insurer is told the travel dates before you go; check the policy covers loss and damage overseas.
Choosing tension or a wide channel or bar band? Get the size right before ordering, as these are the hardest settings to resize later.
White gold rings go back for rhodium replating from time to time; build it into the same visit as the pre-wedding claw check so the ring looks bright in photos.

open_questions.question: Brief's open question answered: GIA confirms tension resizing is 'very difficult, sometimes impossible' (fact_17); the true tension vs tension-style distinction is sourced only to a jeweller's technical page (fact_18), so present it as a 'ask your jeweller which it is' check rather than a gemmological fact.

GIA explicitly names bezel (fact_02) and flush (fact_06) as practical for active wearers; lean on these rather than inventing a ranking. 'Low-set' head height is not given in mm by any source, so keep it relative (lower versus taller head).

assumptions: Fast mode: 15-minute budget; research limited to GIA (4cs.gia.edu, gia.edu), Jewellers Association of Australia, and two jeweller technical pages for definitions.
Gemmological Association of Australia and American Gem Society pages checked but yielded no usable setting-level facts in the time budget.

GIA's 'Most homeowner's and renter's insurance policies' line is US-centric and implies cost; not used. Insurance advice kept to 'check your policy covers loss and damage overseas' (fact_42) and JAA revaluation guidance (fact_43).
Gypsy/burnish naming for flush setting and its suitability for men's or unisex bands is style vocabulary, not a durability claim; no source needed if written as description.
Activity guidance for skiing (gloves), hiking and gym rests on GIA's general statements (fact_02, fact_06, fact_28); specific activity physics is phrased as advice.
